units.label: 共同人格访谈与计分
units.description: 12模型×MBTI/BFI，题项单次回答嵌套于整套测验，整套结果用于RQ1–3。不是每道题独立行为实验。

units.label: RQ0测验知识描述比对
units.description: 模型描述与专家人格定义的词汇/句嵌入相似度，辅助检查测验认知。

units.label: RQ1无条件人格
units.description: 模型、温度下整套测验人格类型频率/BFI均分。

units.label: RQ2人格系统条件
units.description: 16MBTI类型或5BFI因子的人格描述系统条件与无条件对照。

units.label: RQ3人格与职业双条件
units.description: 每个人格/因子加入专家选取的前三职业之一，与人格单条件对照；职业可复用。

facts.statement: 研究RQ0测验知识、RQ1无条件人格稳定性、RQ2人格系统提示的模仿、RQ3再加入人类职业是否改善模仿。MBTI按四二分形成16类，BFI为五连续因子。

method_function.text: 分别操作化分类结果与因子分数，非人类人格效度的直接检验。

facts.statement: Table2的12个现成开放模型为Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1、Llama-2-13b-chat-hf、SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0、Llama-3-8B-Instruct、Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1、Neural-chat-7b-v3-1、Dolphin-2.1-mistral-7b、Vicuna-7b-v1.5、Llama-2-7b-chat-hf、Falcon-7b-instruct、Gemma-1.1-7b-it、Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct；模型已有训练为背景。

method_function.text: 比较不同现成模型；本文实施为推断提示实验。

facts.statement: MBTI采用16personalities网站60题，每题七选项从Agree到Disagree；依该网站参考将整套答案映为人格类别。没有实际付费使用Myers&Briggs基金会约$60/次的工具。

method_function.text: 规定题材、响应空间和类别判定来源。

facts.statement: BFI采用44题1–5级Likert；扩展v3附录F给定五因子题号及反向题R，R题按6−原分反转，再按该因子全部题分平均：Extraversion 8题、Agreeableness 9题、Conscientiousness 9题、Neuroticism 8题、Openness 10题。具体题号见证据，未报无效/缺失回答处理。

method_function.text: 将回答聚合成人格因子量表分数，非概率。

facts.statement: 两测验题目逐个、随机次序提交，以缓解顺序偏差及部分模型上下文限制；统一测验内容和提示设计，但依各模型专用chat template。扩展v3明确每题重新重复条件；仅英语，未将整套问题同次提交。

method_function.text: 实际题序控制和接口适配。

facts.statement: RQ0让模型描述MBTI四二分/16类型与BFI五因子的定义、主要行为例子，再与themyersbriggs.com和John等2008专家描述作词汇与语义相似度比较。

method_function.text: 辅助测验知识检查，不额外招募人类样本。

facts.statement: RQ0在温度.01生成描述；词汇先小写、去标点/停用词及词形归一，再算WO=|s1∩s2|/min(|s1|,|s2|)。语义编码采用现成all-mpnet-base-v2 SentenceTransformer计算余弦。跨模型词重叠MBTI .21/BFI .26、余弦 .67/.66，不能据相似度证明人格理解。

method_function.text: 描述知识匹配的数值，不把相似度直接等同理解。

facts.statement: RQ1无条件提示要求以自身人格选择最贴合选项、不要额外考虑或解释；BFI提示含喜欢与别人相处的示例，再问I see Myself as Someone Who...。

method_function.text: 获取无额外人格条件的自陈式回答。

facts.statement: RQ2系统消息设You are a human，逐一条件化16个MBTI类型，描述含General/Strengths/Potential development/Typical characteristics/Careers/Under stress/Relationships七类；BFI逐一条件化五因子，含verbal labels/conceptual definition/behavioral examples。

method_function.text: 操纵人格描述而非权重训练。

facts.statement: 从StereoSet的120个职业目录，由一组心理学家为每MBTI类型和BFI因子选最相关前三职业；职业可跨人格重复，具体标签与选择结果外指A2–4/A10。扩展v3附录B/D同时列Role Categorization提示，要求从所列职业抽取每类型/因子的前三项；文本未清楚解释该提示与正文心理学家选择的关系，不能擅定为全自动或独立专家一致选择。

method_function.text: 构造职业角色条件，不是120独立实验或新受试者调查。

facts.statement: RQ3以一个已选职业替换RQ2的human身份，并保留目标人格/因子及其描述；Fig3写one Rij(j=1..3)，不是把三职业同时拼接。

method_function.text: 检验职业和人格双重条件相对单人格条件。

facts.statement: 使用AutoGen建立interviewer/interviewee访谈代理，在系统消息保存人格/角色footprint；所有实验经text-generation-webui本地部署，8×NVIDIA A30各24GB、764GB系统内存、96核Xeon和Ubuntu20.04.6。

method_function.text: 实现访谈与提示条件注入。

facts.statement: 两温度为.01/.7。作者称固定top_p和top_k默认值分别50与1（原文如此）；该对应有有效域疑问，未擅自交换成top_k50/top_p1。

method_function.text: 报告生成设置并保留来源冲突。

facts.statement: RQ1每模型/温度重复N次，冻结文未数值化N；RQ2–3每模型/温度/人格或因子称N=30，给12×2×16×30=11520MBTI及12×2×5×30=3600BFI总测验。总式未显式乘三角色或两种协议，不能合并推算RQ3测试总数。

method_function.text: 辨明题目、整套重复、模型/温度/人格条件层次。

facts.statement: RQ1按重复整套测验输出统计MBTI类型相对频率与BFI五因子N次平均分，图4/5分别呈两温度；BFI轴为1–5分数。

method_function.text: 概括无条件测验分布，非回答置信概率。

facts.statement: 无条件低温常见ENFJ，J在模型中占优势；升温部分模型更多样，Falcon可出现12类型，但Llama家族/Gemma/Phi3仍偏ENFJ；作者报告两温度均无ISTP/INFP/INTP。BFI多因子分高而Neuroticism通常较低。

method_function.text: 报告样本内输出模式。

facts.statement: RQ2以输出MBTI是否吻合指定类别的准确率对N次重复求平均；Table3左表同时列均值±标准差，但冻结文未明确SD跨人格还是跨重复的精确计算层次。右表为目标BFI分数相对无条件值的百分比变化。

method_function.text: 区分类别命中与连续分数基线变化。

facts.statement: RQ2MBTI表3：SOLAR两温度.785±.391/.744±.353，Dolphin .654±.459/.633±.379；多模型低命中。BFI如Llama3Neuroticism低温变化233.3%，文中perfect指目标因子分到5，非总体人格测量完全有效。

method_function.text: 保留代表结果及计分解释边界。

facts.statement: RQ3作者报告SOLAR/NeuralChat/Llama3/Dolphin的MBTI模仿有改善，teacher关联ENFJ在约9/12模型近乎完全命中；BFI部分因子改善但两Llama的Agreeableness及Falcon等可下降。扩展v3 Table7列各模型×两温度×人格×三职业的MBTI平均命中，连字符代0；Table8列对应BFI相对无条件的百分增长，含负值，不是原始因子分或概率。

method_function.text: 报告双条件的异质性而非保证改善。

facts.statement: 作者将Mixtral的INFJ偏好与混合专家架构相联系，并将多数模型抗人格条件描述为closed-minded；也把较大SD解释为模仿难度而非统计可靠性不足。这些均为解释，未实施架构干预或可靠性证明。

method_function.text: 将结果与作者机制/人格解释分开。

facts.statement: 作者因硬件限制选可部署模型，对训练数据/方法影响不能量化；没有本文人格数据微调，fine-tuning/alignment为未来研究。GPT4o只指向扩展A13，冻结正文未展示其结果，不能计入12开放模型实验分母。

evidence.quote:
Administering the Tests
Each of the two tests consists of a set of questions and a
set of options as valid answers. The MBTI test provides a
set QMBTI of 60 questions through the www.16Personalities.
com platform, a well-known relevant resource for MBTI,
which are listed in Extended Ver. A3. An LLM is required
to select an answer from OMBTI = {Agree, Generally Agree,
Partially Agree, Neither Agree nor Disagree, Partially Disagree, Generally Disagree, Disagree}. Answers are then
evaluated according to the 16Personalities reference in order to associate a model with one MBTI personality.
Likewise, the BFI test utilized in this study provides a
set QBFI of 44 questions as defined in (John and Srivastava
1999), which are listed in Extended Ver. A5. An LLM is required to select an answer from OBFI ={Disagree strongly,
Disagree a little, Neither agree nor disagree, Agree a little, Agree strongly}. The answers, which are associated
with a Likert-scale (from 1: Disagree strongly to 5: Agree
strongly) are then evaluated according to a predefined set of
rules (John and Srivastava 1999), which eventually assign
each individual to an aggregated score for each of the five
personality factors. An overview of the steps performed to
obtain the final scores is given in Extended Ver. A6.
To mitigate potential biases due to the ordering of
prompts (Zhao et al. 2021) and to accommodate the limited
context attention of some LLMs, for both tests we administered the questions individually and in a random order.

Agent Creation and Models Deployment
To set up our LLM personality assessment as a psychological interview, we treated our selected models as interviewee and interviewer agents. To this aim, we leveraged the
open-source AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023) framework, which
enables us to declare a system message to associate each
agent with certain personalities or roles according to our described methodology, thus effectively providing each agent
with a “footprint” that determines and keeps its behavior coherent during interactions.
For each considered model, we kept the top p and top k
parameters at their default values of 50 and 1, respectively,
as temperature impacts on the model’s creativity (Chen and
Ding 2023) by acting directly on the shape of the probability
distribution rather than the considered tokens, thus avoiding
adding further complexity and making reproducibility easier
to carry out. Additionally, we refrained from altering both
temperature and top p, as such simultaneous adjustment is
typically discouraged to prevent disruptive effects on the
delicate balance between diversity and coherence.
We carried out all our experiments locally by deploying
our models through the open-source text-generation-webui
framework,2 using a 8x NVIDIA A30 GPU server with 24
GB of RAM each, 764 GB of system RAM, a Double Intel
Xeon Gold 6248R with a total of 96 cores, and Ubuntu Linux
20.04.6 LTS as operating system.

Temperature and Repetitions
To make our assessments of the models’ personalities statistically meaningful, we conducted multiple independent repetitions of the MBTI test, resp. BFI test, for each model and
temperature setting. The latter implies considering the impact of model temperature on the generated outputs (i.e.,
higher resp. lower values correspond to more creative/diversified resp. more deterministic and focused behavior). To assess RQ1, we carried out the N repetitions of either test on
each model using two distinct temperature values, namely
τ = {0.01, 0.7}, then we finally counted the outcomes on
QMBTI , resp. QBFI , over the N repetitions per temperature.
To assess RQ2-RQ3, we tested each model, for each temperature τ = {0.01, 0.7} and each personality in P M BT I ,
resp. P BF I , with N = 30 independent repetitions, for a total of 12 × 2 × 16 × 30 = 11, 520 independent MBTI tests
and 12 × 2 × 5 × 30 = 3, 600 independent BFI tests.

Awareness Check
Our investigation of the personality-mimicking capabilities
of LLMs starts by answering a preliminary research question
(RQ0): whether and to what extent such LLMs are aware
of the MBTI and BFI tests. To this purpose, we conducted
a semi-qualitative assessment on how the LLMs selected
in our study are informed about (i) for MBTI, the four dichotomies and the resulting 16 personality types associated,
and (ii) for BFI, the five factors, their definition, and their

main behavioral examples. Our analysis focused on evaluating the lexical and semantic similarity between the description associated by each model to the set of MBTI personalities, resp. BFI factors, and the “ground-truth” description of
the latter provided by domain experts (themyersbriggs.com
for MBTI and (John, Naumann, and Soto 2008) for BFI).

LLM agents are found to be aware of the MBTI and BFI
tests, as indicated by a moderately high semantic similarity
of 0.67 and 0.66, respectively, based on the cosine similarity
of the description’s encodings obtained through a Sentence
Transformer model. This compensates for a low lexical overlap of 0.21, resp. 0.26, hinting at a jargon used by the LLMs
that differs from the reference descriptions of MBTI personalities and BFI factors, respectively. Due to space limitations
of this paper, we refer the reader to Extended Ver. A1 for details.

Unconditioned Prompting. To answer our RQ1, we subjected each model to the MBTI test, resp. the BFI test, by
administering the set of questions QMBTI , resp. QBFI using
unconditioned instruction prompting, which strictly adhere
to the MBTI, resp. BFI, templates, as shown in Fig. 1.

Temperature and Repetitions
To make our assessments of the models’ personalities statistically meaningful, we conducted multiple independent repetitions of the MBTI test, resp. BFI test, for each model and
temperature setting. The latter implies considering the impact of model temperature on the generated outputs (i.e.,
higher resp. lower values correspond to more creative/diversified resp. more deterministic and focused behavior). To assess RQ1, we carried out the N repetitions of either test on
each model using two distinct temperature values, namely
τ = {0.01, 0.7}, then we finally counted the outcomes on
QMBTI , resp. QBFI , over the N repetitions per temperature.

Personalities of LLMs
In addressing our main research questions RQ1-RQ3, we
devised three prompting strategies when administering the

that we meticulously followed the MBTI question set, resp.

equally in terms of prompting, in the respect of each LLM’s
usage instructions. (Each LLM has indeed its own chat template to handle conversations, and we ensured compliance
with these specific requirements for each model.)

We summarize here main findings about our evaluation
of RQ3; comprehensive results are reported in Extended
Ver. A10.

cator (MBTI) and Big Five Inventory (BFI), we aim to answer the following research questions:
RQ0 — Are LLM agents aware of the MBTI and BFI psychological tests?
RQ1 — Do LLM agents consistently exhibit personality
traits according to MBTI and BFI?
RQ2 — Can LLM agents mimic specific personality traits
through system prompting?
RQ3 — Do LLM agents improve their mimicking capabilities when instructed to act according to specific
human roles?
To address the above RQs, we create a family of 12 LLM
agents built upon the most representative Open LLMs available to date, and we subject them to human-like interviews
to assess their personalities under different experimental
scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first
to conduct an extensive analysis of recent LLMs on both
MBTI and BFI tests aimed at answering all above RQs. This
differs from previous research that (i) focused either on a
single model or test, (ii) was conducted on “outdated” or
closed models only, and (iii) used different methodological
approaches, as we shall detail in the next sections.

The MBTI test is a self-report personality assessment
questionnaire (Myers 1962, 1985), which gauges four dichotomies and shapes 16 distinct personalities (Table 1), encompassing strengths, weaknesses, and peculiar behaviors
of each personality. The categorical nature of MBTI (where
each individual pertains to a unique category) enables us to
frame the assessment as a multi-class classification problem
for answering our RQs.
BFI (John and Srivastava 1999) identifies five core factors, namely Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion,
Agreeableness, and Neuroticism, so that a personality type
can be characterized by varying degrees of such factors. BFI
is most widely used in academic psychology and, differently
from MBTI, it measures personality traits on a scale rather
than grouping them into binary categories. In this respect,
to address our RQs we shall take a different evaluation perspective w.r.t. the one for MBTI.

Our study involves a representative body of the Open LLM
landscape, varying by sizes and architectures, for which we
accessed their publicly available implementations on the
HuggingFace Model Hub as of early 2024. Table 2 summarizes the main characteristics of the LLMs selected in
this study, namely the uncensored Dolphin in its 7B version,
Gemma (Team 2024), Falcon (Almazrouei et al. 2023) in its

Agent Creation and Models Deployment
To set up our LLM personality assessment as a psychological interview, we treated our selected models as interviewee and interviewer agents. To this aim, we leveraged the
open-source AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023) framework, which
enables us to declare a system message to associate each
agent with certain personalities or roles according to our described methodology, thus effectively providing each agent
with a “footprint” that determines and keeps its behavior coherent during interactions.
For each considered model, we kept the top p and top k
parameters at their default values of 50 and 1, respectively,
as temperature impacts on the model’s creativity (Chen and
Ding 2023) by acting directly on the shape of the probability
distribution rather than the considered tokens, thus avoiding
adding further complexity and making reproducibility easier
to carry out. Additionally, we refrained from altering both
temperature and top p, as such simultaneous adjustment is
typically discouraged to prevent disruptive effects on the
delicate balance between diversity and coherence.
We carried out all our experiments locally by deploying
our models through the open-source text-generation-webui
framework,2 using a 8x NVIDIA A30 GPU server with 24
GB of RAM each, 764 GB of system RAM, a Double Intel
Xeon Gold 6248R with a total of 96 cores, and Ubuntu Linux
20.04.6 LTS as operating system.

Temperature and Repetitions
To make our assessments of the models’ personalities statistically meaningful, we conducted multiple independent repetitions of the MBTI test, resp. BFI test, for each model and
temperature setting. The latter implies considering the impact of model temperature on the generated outputs (i.e.,
higher resp. lower values correspond to more creative/diversified resp. more deterministic and focused behavior). To assess RQ1, we carried out the N repetitions of either test on
each model using two distinct temperature values, namely
τ = {0.01, 0.7}, then we finally counted the outcomes on
QMBTI , resp. QBFI , over the N repetitions per temperature.
To assess RQ2-RQ3, we tested each model, for each temperature τ = {0.01, 0.7} and each personality in P M BT I ,
resp. P BF I , with N = 30 independent repetitions, for a total of 12 × 2 × 16 × 30 = 11, 520 independent MBTI tests
and 12 × 2 × 5 × 30 = 3, 600 independent BFI tests.

which means a tendency to be self-confident, goal-oriented,
systematic, and objective decision-maker.

Our research questions shed light on the emergence of a
footprint identity among LLMs based on their distinguishable intrinsic personality types, with a notable heterogeneity in how these models mirror human personality traits
through prompt conditioning on specific personalities and
roles. Models such as SOLAR, Dolphin, NeuralChat, and
Llama3-8 have demonstrated remarkable mimicking capabilities, while the majority rather show closed-mindedness.
We believe that our findings might serve for assisting a responsible development of human-like computational agents.

Challenges in models’ deployment. While some of the
models used in this work are also available in larger sizes,
e.g., Falcon 180B, Llama3-70B and Llama2-65B, deploying
them poses challenges due to higher computational requirements for our hardware, including excessive quantization.
To prevent performance degradation and ensure easier reproducibility, we focused on models with more manageable deployments. This decision does not compromise our findings,
as smaller models have been recognized to excel in benchmarks (e.g., AlpacaEval — Community tab) and might be
comparable to larger models (Abdin et al. 2024).

Closed models? It should be emphasized that our approach and evaluation methodology are equally applicable
to closed models (cf. Extended Ver. A13 for results on the
new GPT-4o). Nonetheless, in the spirit of open science, we
chose to focus on open LLMs for their greater transparency,
local execution capabilities, and customization options, enabling more in-depth and cost-effective investigations.
Our future research involves fine-tuning and aligning
open LLMs with personality-aware data. This will enhance
the simulation of human traits, aiming at developing models

F Scoring the BFI Test
To score the BFI tests administered to our models, we meticulously followed the original procedure
described in (John and Srivastava, 1999). Each of the 44 BFI questions listed in Table 6 contributes to the
score of a specific factor, as detailed below:
• Extraversion: 1, 6R, 11, 16, 21R, 26, 31R, 36
• Agreeableness: 2R, 7, 12R, 17, 22, 27R, 32, 37R, 42
• Conscientiousness: 3, 8R, 13, 18R, 23R, 28, 33, 38, 43R
• Neuroticism: 4, 9R, 14, 19, 24R, 29, 34R, 39
• Openness: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35R, 40, 41R, 44
Note that symbol “R” is used to indicate those questions that relate negatively to the corresponding
factor, therefore their values are scored in a reverse way (for example, if the score to an answer to question
31 is 4, then the actual score is to be calculated as 6-4=2).
The final score for each factor is calculated by averaging all the values associated with that factor.

such a limitation we also mitigate potential biases
in the ordering of questions (Zhao et al., 2021).

exclusively in English. Results may differ in other
languages, and extending the test to multiple languages using multilingual capable models could
reveal variations in outcomes based on linguistic

Further Results from the Personality-Conditioned MBTI tests

We discuss here remarks that can be drawn from Figs. 12–23 on the behaviors of the models w.r.t. their
architectural commonalities.
A prominent example is SOLAR, which outperforms Llama2-7 despite being built on that; this might
be ascribed to a combination of optimizations (Kim et al., 2023) that include (i) initializing the model
with pre-trained weights from Mistral 7B, (ii) employing the Depth Up-Scaling, and (iii) leveraging a
more effective mixture of datasets. Similarly, Dolphin demonstrates striking improvement over Mistral,
despite being derived from it: in this case, the performance differences should depend on the absence of
“alignment”, an inherent awareness designed to prevent models from engaging in undesirable behavior,
potentially allowing Dolphin to discern more subtleties and exhibit greater flexibility in emulating specific
human personalities. Besides this, Dolphin was trained on the Airoboros and Samantha DNA datasets,
aimed at increasing creativity and empathy, respectively,8 reasonably improving its human mimicking
capabilities. A further intriguing scenario involves NeuralChat, which outperforms Mistral despite being
based on it. This enhancement can be attributed to the fine-tuning process using the higher-quality
SlimOrca dataset (Lian et al., 2023), as well as the implementation of a specifically crafted Direct
Preference Optimization (DPO) phase,9 designed to better align the model with human preferences.
As a side yet relevant remark, it is worth noticing that although the 13B version of Llama2 behaves
slightly worse than its smaller 7B variant, while Llama3-8 outperforms both. The lack of strong correlation
that might be ascribed to the impact of the model size is further supported by the inferior performances of
Mixtral (with approximately 47B) when compared to the top-performing model SOLAR, having only a
quarter of the parameters.
